author: historian-agent:mig-1
title: Austronesian expansion from Taiwan
summary: Farming communities in Taiwan, speakers of early Austronesian languages, began moving south about 4,000-5,000 years ago through the Philippines and island Southeast Asia and later across the Pacific. One arm, from southern Borneo, reached Madagascar in the first millennium CE, a date that is still contested.

uncertainty.note: Taiwan Neolithic from about 5,500/5,000 BP (year -3300 is the midpoint 5,250 BP); the expansion out of Taiwan is dated about 4,200/4,000 BP. Philippines: related pottery assemblages between 2500 and 1500 BC (ANU Press). Madagascar: the linguistic estimate is 1,450-1,350 BP (year 550); archaeological claims range from 10,000 BP to almost 1,000 BP, with a consensus of about 2,000-1,600 BP (Hixon et al. 2021) cited by the Oxford Handbook. This record follows only the western arm; the Pacific arm is covered by the Lapita and Polynesian records.

as_recorded.value: Neolithic cultures in Taiwan with pottery and rice and millet cultivation from about 5,500/5,000 BP; expansion well dated as starting around 4,200/4,000 BP
Between 2500 and 1500 BC related assemblages with plain or red-slipped pottery appeared in the Philippines, Sulawesi, northern Borneo and Halmahera
Austronesian migration to Madagascar began ca. 1,450-1,350 BP, from the Barito River area of Borneo; archaeological consensus around 2,000-1,600 BP

when.display: c. 3300 BCE to 550 CE (Madagascar arm contested)

where.historical_name: Neolithic Taiwan, before the Austronesian dispersal; no recorded place names

waypoints.label: Taiwan: Neolithic farmers with pottery, rice and millet, regarded as the source of the expansion. Point is the island centroid.
Philippines: related pottery assemblages appear in coastal regions. Point is the national centroid; individual sites are not named in the source.

waypoints.date: ca. 1,450-1,350 BP (start of migration to Madagascar, Oxford Handbook)
waypoints.label: Barito River area, South Kalimantan, Borneo: the Malagasy language derives from South East Barito languages of this area. Date is a linguistic estimate for the departure.

waypoints.date: ca. 1,450-1,350 BP (linguistic estimate); contested: archaeological claims range from 10,000 BP to almost 1,000 BP, with a 2,000-1,600 BP consensus
waypoints.label: Madagascar: settled by Austronesian speakers and, by genetics, by people with Bantu-related ancestry. Point is the island centre.

importance.justification: Created the widest-ranging language family and carried farming and seafaring from Madagascar to Polynesia.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the Philippines waypoint is a country centroid with a range-only date; the Barito and Madagascar waypoints share one year (the date is a linguistic estimate, and archaeology disagrees); the route skips Sulawesi and the Pacific arm; the Taiwan midpoint blends two date estimates. Needs a source naming Batanes or Luzon sites (e.g. Nagsabaran).

beats.caption: Rice and millet farmers with pottery live in Taiwan, the setting from which Austronesian-speaking groups spread out around 4,200-4,000 years ago.
Related pottery traditions appear in the Philippines, Sulawesi, northern Borneo and Halmahera as voyagers move south.
Settlers from southern Borneo reach Madagascar; its language descends from the Barito River region. Dating is debated.
